n: Nahum’s message is a “burden” — a heavy oracle — against Nineveh, capital of Assyria. About a century after Jonah, Nineveh had returned to cruelty. Nahum likely spoke between 663 and 612 BC, when Nineveh fell.

f.g: A weighty prophetic message, usually of judgment.
His name means “comfort” — his message comforted Judah, oppressed by Assyria.
From Elkosh, a village whose location is uncertain.

n: God is fiercely protective of His people and will repay His enemies. His “vengeance” is not petty revenge but justice against oppressors who refuse to repent.

f.g: Zealous, passionately devoted to His covenant people.

n: God is patient, but He won’t let the guilty go unpunished forever. His power shows in storms; the clouds are just dust kicked up by His feet.

f.w: The LORD is slow to anger
the clouds are the dust of his feet
f.g: A striking image of God’s greatness: storm clouds are like dust from His steps.

n: He commands the sea and dries up rivers, as at the Red Sea and Jordan. Even the most fertile places — Bashan, Carmel, Lebanon — wither before Him.

f.g: Rich pasture land east of the Sea of Galilee.

n: Mountains shake and hills melt in His presence; the whole earth trembles.
Who can withstand His anger? His fury pours out like fire and shatters rocks.
Yet in the middle of the storm: “The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble.” He knows and cares for those who trust Him. The same power that judges protects.

f.w: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble
he knoweth them that trust in him

n: With an overwhelming flood He will end Nineveh. Ancient sources report that flooding helped breach Nineveh’s defenses in 612 BC.
Whatever Assyria plots against the Lord will fail. He will finish it so completely that trouble won’t need to come twice.

f.w: What do ye imagine against the LORD?

n: Like tangled thorns and staggering drunks, the enemies will be burned up like dry straw.

f.g: Entangled like thornbushes — which burn quickly.

n: A wicked counselor came from Nineveh who plotted against the Lord — perhaps King Sennacherib, who besieged Jerusalem.
Though Assyria is strong and numerous, it will be cut down. To Judah, God says: “I afflicted you, but I won’t afflict you anymore.”

f.w: I will afflict thee no more

n: God will break Assyria’s yoke off Judah’s neck and snap the chains of their oppression.

f.w: I break his yoke from off thee

n: To Assyria’s king God decrees: your dynasty will end, your idols will be destroyed, and I will prepare your grave.

f.w: no more of thy name be sown
f.g: You will have no descendants to carry on your name.

n: Look! A messenger runs across the mountains with good news of peace. Judah can again celebrate its feasts, for the oppressor is gone. Isaiah used the same words, and Abinadi applied them to those who publish the gospel.

f.w: the feet of him that bringeth good tidings
